title_ur: ہزاروں خواہشیں ایسی کہ ہر خواہش پہ دم نکلے
title_roman: hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ aisī ki har ḳhvāhish pe dam nikle
source: Text and transliteration: Rekhta, via github.com/amir9ume/urdu_ghazals_rekhta

overview.summary: The ghazal is built around the refrain 'nikle' (came out/emerged), giving each couplet a sense of something issuing forth: desires, blood, disgrace, secrets, the pen, the wine-cup, cruelty, life-breath, and the preacher's path. Its couplets are linked less by a single narrative than by this refrain and an ironic, melancholy voice complaining of love, fate, and social hypocrisy. Ghalib contrasts the lover's suffering and disgrace with the beloved's indifference and the preacher's false piety, ending on a wry note about the distance between the tavern and the pulpit.

ur: ہزاروں خواہشیں ایسی کہ ہر خواہش پہ دم نکلے
بہت نکلے مرے ارمان لیکن پھر بھی کم نکلے
roman: hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ aisī ki har ḳhvāhish pe dam nikle
bahut nikle mire armān lekin phir bhī kam nikle

phrases.gloss: the breath would leave; one would die

poetic: Thousands of desires, each such that at every desire one would die;
Many of my longings came out, yet even so they came out few.
notes: dam nikalnā is an idiom for dying; here the subjunctive dam nikle makes each desire a potential death.
The refrain nikle shifts sense: in line 0 it is the breath leaving the body, in line 1 it is longings being fulfilled or expressed.
hazāroñ ḳhvāhisheñ is hyperbolic, not a literal count; it conveys endless, overwhelming desire.
armān and ḳhvāhish are near-synonyms, binding the two lines through repeated longing.
The irony is that even bahut (many) fulfilled desires feel kam (few), because desire itself is limitless.

context_notes.text: The verb nikle is used for breath leaving the body in dam nikalnā (to die) and for longings being fulfilled or expressed.

ur: ڈرے کیوں میرا قاتل کیا رہے گا اس کی گردن پر
وہ خوں جو چشم تر سے عمر بھر یوں دم بدم نکلے
roman: Dare kyuuñ merā qātil kyā rahegā us kī gardan par
vo ḳhuuñ jo chashm-e-tar se umr bhar yuuñ dam-ba-dam nikle

phrases.gloss: will remain on his neck, will be held against him

poetic: Why should my killer fear? What will remain upon his neck—
that blood which from wet eyes, all life, kept issuing moment by moment?
notes: The question is ironic: the beloved as killer sheds no actual blood, only the lover's tears, so no stain of murder remains on the beloved's neck.
ḳhuuñ here means the blood-like tears that flow from the lover's eyes; he has wept all his life.
gardan par rahegā carries the idiomatic sense of guilt or a blood-debt being held against someone.
chashm-e-tar is a Persian-style compound meaning wet or weeping eyes.
dam-ba-dam, literally breath by breath, intensifies the refrain nikle: the tears or blood issue constantly, moment after moment.

context_notes.text: In ghazal convention the beloved is often called the lover's qātil (killer); the lover dies from the beloved's cruelty.

ur: نکلنا خلد سے آدم کا سنتے آئے ہیں لیکن
بہت بے آبرو ہو کر ترے کوچے سے ہم نکلے
roman: nikalnā ḳhuld se aadam kā sunte aa.e haiñ lekin
bahut be-ābrū ho kar tire kūche se ham nikle

units.gloss: Paradise, the garden from which Adam was expelled

phrases.gloss: we have always heard; it has come down to us by tradition

poetic: We have always heard the tale of Adam's going out from Paradise—
but from your lane I came out utterly dishonoured.
notes: The phrase khuld se aadam kā nikalnā refers to the Quranic/Islamic story of Adam's expulsion from Paradise.
sunte aa.e haiñ is an idiom meaning 'we have heard from old' or 'tradition tells us', not literally 'we have come hearing'.
ābrū literally means the water or brightness of the face, hence honour; be-ābrū means stripped of face/honour, disgraced.
The beloved's kūcha is placed above Paradise: leaving it in disgrace is treated as a fall greater than Adam's.
The refrain nikalnā/nikle links Adam's expulsion to the lover's departure, both being an emergence from grace into loss.

context_notes.text: In Islamic tradition, Adam was expelled from Paradise (khuld); the line refers to this story.

ur: بھرم کھل جائے ظالم تیرے قامت کی درازی کا
اگر اس طرۂ پر پیچ و خم کا پیچ و خم نکلے
roman: bharam khul jaa.e zālim tere qāmat kī darāzī kā
agar is turra-e-pur-pech-o-ḳham kā pech-o-ḳham nikle

units.gloss: forelock tress full of twists and curls

phrases.gloss: for an illusion or secret to be exposed
for twists and curls to come out or be undone

literal.text: tress full of twists and curls

poetic: The illusion of your tallness would be exposed, O cruel one—
if ever the twists and curls of this curl-laden tress were straightened out.
notes: The idiom 'bharam khulnā' means to have one's illusion, secret, or deception exposed.
The beloved's tall stature (qāmat kī darāzī) is a standard image of beauty, here treated as a false impression created by the curled tress.
The compound 'turra-e-pur-pech-o-kham' already contains the word 'pech-o-kham', so the line literally repeats the idea: the twist of a tress full of twist.
The refrain word 'nikle' here carries the sense of being straightened or released, not merely emerging.
'zālim' is vocative: the lover addresses the beloved as a beautiful but cruel tyrant.

context_notes.text: The beloved's tall stature (qāmat kī darāzī) is a standard image of beauty in ghazal convention.
The word pech-o-kham (twists and curls) occurs within turra-e-pur-pech-o-kham and is then repeated as a separate noun.
The beloved is addressed as zālim (cruel one/tyrant), a conventional way to address the cruel beloved.

ur: مگر لکھوائے کوئی اس کو خط تو ہم سے لکھوائے
ہوئی صبح اور گھر سے کان پر رکھ کر قلم نکلے
roman: magar likhvā.e koī us ko ḳhat to ham se likhvā.e
huī sub.h aur ghar se kaan par rakh kar qalam nikle

phrases.gloss: with it placed on/behind the ear

literal.text: if someone should have him write a letter

poetic: But if someone would have him write a letter, then let it be written by us;
Morning came, and from the house he came out with a pen behind his ear.
notes: ḳhat primarily means letter here, but in ghazal vocabulary it also suggests the first down on the beloved's cheek and a line of writing, making the beloved's letter as precious as her down.
The pen placed on the ear is the badge of a professional scribe; the lover presents himself as ready to write for the beloved at dawn.
The repeated causative likhvā.e is pointed: the beloved will not write herself, someone must be made to write, and the poet insists that someone should be him.
huī sub.h is an idiom for daybreak; the second line answers the first with a scene of the lover already out with pen behind ear as soon as morning comes.
The couplet plays on the beloved's letter as a longed-for object; the lover would even serve as its scribe just to be near those words.

context_notes.text: The word ḳhat means letter, but in ghazal vocabulary it also means the first down on a beloved's cheek and a line of writing.
A pen placed behind the ear was the badge of a professional scribe.

ur: ہوئی اس دور میں منسوب مجھ سے بادہ آشامی
پھر آیا وہ زمانہ جو جہاں میں جام جم نکلے
roman: huī is daur meñ mansūb mujh se bāda-ashāmī
phir aayā vo zamāna jo jahāñ meñ jām-e-jam nikle
poetic: In this age, wine-drinking is attributed to me—
again has come that age when in the world Jamshid’s cup comes forth.
notes: bāda-ashāmī (wine-drinking) carries the Sufi sense of drinking the wine of divine love, so the accusation may be spiritual, not literal.
jām-e-jam is the world-revealing cup of the legendary king Jamshid; its emergence signals a return of a visionary or mystical age.
The couplet turns on the refrain nikle: the speaker's reputation 'comes out' as a wine-drinker just as the legendary cup 'comes forth' into the world.
mansūb mujh se implies an imputed or attributed connection, often with a hint of false accusation or notoriety.
The juxtaposition of the speaker's alleged drinking and the reappearance of Jamshid's cup suggests that the present age is one of unveiling, not mere drunkenness.

context_notes.text: In Sufi poetry, bāda-ashāmī (wine-drinking) can mean drinking the wine of divine love, not literal wine.
Jām-e-jam is the world-revealing cup of the legendary king Jamshid; its appearance signals a visionary age.

ur: ہوئی جن سے توقع خستگی کی داد پانے کی
وہ ہم سے بھی زیادہ خستۂ تیغ ستم نکلے
roman: huī jin se tavaqqo ḳhastagī kī daad paane kī
vo ham se bhī ziyāda ḳhasta-e-teġh-e-sitam nikle

literal.text: wounded by the sword of cruelty

poetic: Those from whom we expected to receive sympathy for our woundedness—
they turned out even more wounded by the sword of cruelty than us.
notes: The idiom 'daad paana' means to receive justice or praise; here it shades into receiving sympathy or recognition for one's wounds.
The Persian izafat chain 'ḳhasta-e teġh-e sitam' intensifies the wound by naming its source as the sword of cruelty.
The refrain word 'nikle' in this couplet carries the sense 'turned out' or 'proved to be', not merely 'came out'.
The couplet's irony undercuts the speaker's self-pity: the people expected to console him are even more wounded by cruelty than he is.
The construction 'jin se tavaqqo ... paane kī' is inverted in English; the expectation is of receiving appreciation for woundedness.

ur: محبت میں نہیں ہے فرق جینے اور مرنے کا
اسی کو دیکھ کر جیتے ہیں جس کافر پہ دم نکلے
roman: mohabbat meñ nahīñ hai farq jiine aur marne kā
usī ko dekh kar jiite haiñ jis kāfir pe dam nikle
poetic: In love there is no difference between living and dying—
we live by seeing that very infidel for whom the breath departs.
notes: The idiom 'dam nikalnā' means to die or breathe one's last, so the beloved is the one for whom the lover dies.
'Kāfir' here is the beloved, not a religious infidel; in ghazal convention the beloved is cruel, faithless, and worshipped by the lover.
The couplet turns on paradox: love makes living and dying the same, since the lover lives only by gazing at the beloved who causes his death.
The relative clause 'usī ko... jis kāfir pe' links the act of living to the very infidel for whom the breath departs.

context_notes.text: In ghazal convention the beloved is called kāfir (infidel); here it means the cruel, faithless beloved, not a religious infidel.

ur: کہاں مے خانہ کا دروازہ غالبؔ اور کہاں واعظ
پر اتنا جانتے ہیں کل وہ جاتا تھا کہ ہم نکلے
roman: kahāñ mai-ḳhāne kā darvāza 'ġhālib' aur kahāñ vaa.iz
par itnā jānte haiñ kal vo jaatā thā ki ham nikle

phrases.gloss: idiom 'where ... and where ...' implying vast separation or lack of comparison

poetic: Where is the tavern's door, Ghalib—and where the preacher!
But this much I know: yesterday he was heading there as I came out.
notes: The idiom 'kahāñ ... aur kahāñ' signals that the two things named have almost no relation or can hardly be compared.
This is the maqta, the final couplet in which Ghalib signs his pen name and closes with an ironic thrust at the preacher's secret leaning toward the tavern.
The word 'kal' can mean yesterday or tomorrow, but the past tense 'jaatā thā' fixes it here as yesterday.
The tavern (mai-ḳhāne) symbolises forbidden pleasure or spiritual intoxication, standing in opposition to the orthodox preacher (vaaʿiz).
The refrain 'nikle' lands the line's wit: just as the poet emerges, the preacher is seen heading in, reversing the moral arrangement.

context_notes.text: This is the maqta, the final couplet where the poet traditionally inserts his pen name; here Ghalib names himself.
The word kal can mean yesterday or tomorrow; the past tense jaatā thā fixes it as yesterday.
The tavern (mai-khāne) and the preacher (vāʿiz) are conventional opposites in ghazal poetry; the tavern symbolizes forbidden or spiritual intoxication.
